analysis.one_liner: Extends Social Security and Medicare payroll taxes to income above $400,000 to shore up the trust funds.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 5 Democratic sponsors, sent to the Senate Finance Committee, and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill raises the money that funds Social Security and Medicare by applying the payroll tax to wages, self-employment income, and investment income above $400,000 a year, amounts that currently escape these taxes. It also applies the tax to pass-through business income of high earners, closing a route that lets professionals and business owners classify salary as business profits to avoid payroll taxes. The new revenue is deposited directly into the Social Security and Medicare trust funds. The bill never advanced past its referral to the Finance Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Social Security and Medicare beneficiaries, and workers who will depend on those programs, gain because the new revenue extends the life of the trust funds that pay their benefits. Workers at all income levels are unaffected, since the new taxes apply only above $400,000.

how_it_helps.text: Extends the Social Security payroll tax to wages between the current taxable maximum and $400,000, so high earners pay into the system on income that is now exempt.
Adds a 1.2% Medicare tax on wages and self-employment income above $400,000 (with no upper limit), strengthening the hospital insurance fund.

Applies payroll and investment taxes to pass-through business income of taxpayers earning over $400,000, ending the practice of classifying earned income as distributed business profits to escape the tax.
Directs the new investment-income tax revenue into the Social Security, disability, and Medicare hospital insurance trust funds (71.3%, 10.3%, and 28.7% respectively).

analysis.who_pays: Households and pass-through business owners earning over $400,000 a year, who would pay payroll taxes on income currently above the cap, an additional 1.2% Medicare tax, and a higher 17.4% net investment income tax, including on income currently shielded by business classification.

drawbacks.text: The tax falls on pass-through business owners, including owners of smaller professional firms, partnerships, and family businesses earning over $400,000, who would see a direct tax increase on income they currently structure to avoid payroll taxes.

Extending payroll taxes above the current wage cap changes the historical link between taxes paid and benefits earned; the bill text does not explain how benefits would be credited for the newly taxed income, raising questions high earners and their employers would raise in any markup.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill directs a large, dedicated revenue stream into two programs that tens of millions of retirees and disabled workers rely on, paid entirely by households earning over $400,000 who now stop paying these taxes past their first ~$160,000 of wages. The main cost is a real tax increase on high-income professionals and business owners, which supporters would argue merely ends a carve-out; the main design risk is the unresolved question of how benefits are credited on newly taxed income above the cap.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, referred to the Senate Finance Committee, and sat there with no hearing, markup, or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse introduced the Medicare and Social Security Fair Share Act on April 18, 2023.
Four Democratic senators cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day it was introduced.
That referral was the last action on the bill; the Finance Committee took it up no further, and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Households and pass-through business owners earning over $400,000 keep paying no Social Security or Medicare payroll tax on income above the current wage cap, and the trust funds' funding gap remains unaddressed by this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners and pass-through business owners

for.name: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to extend payroll and investment taxes above $400,000 to fund Social Security and Medicare.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on April 18, 2023 and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; that referral was the bill's final action.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: None of the 49 Republican senators cosponsored the bill, signaling no cross-party path to a vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 5 sponsors were Democrats (the sponsor plus 4 of 48 Senate Democrats); no Republican cosponsored, and no vote was ever taken to reveal a fuller partisan split.

industries.industry: Pass-through business owners (law firms, partnerships, hedge funds, private equity)
industries.note: The bill applies payroll taxes to pass-through income of owners earning over $400,000, eliminating the current advantage of classifying earned income as distributed business profits. These owners currently escape the roughly 15% payroll tax on such income.

Would pay Social Security payroll tax on wages between the current cap and $400,000, a 1.2% additional Medicare tax above the threshold, and a 17.4% investment income tax. The revenue funds programs that benefit the broader public.
The Medicare hospital insurance trust fund receives 28.7% of the new investment tax revenue, shoring up payments to hospitals and other providers and the program's solvency.
